title: Practicing forgiveness
hook: forgiveness is a decision before it's a feeling
tomorrow: why would Jesus tell you to walk out in the middle of worship?

segments.voice: Yesterday, those who disagree: you can hold your ground and still refuse to look down on the other person. The line was without contempt.

The sorry arrives by text. You type it's fine, delete it, type it again. It isn't fine yet. Genesis has a scene that starts right about there. Joseph's brothers once sold him as a slave. Years later he runs Egypt for Pharaoh, and he has fed the whole family through a famine. Then their father Jacob dies, and the brothers panic. Maybe Joseph was only waiting for this. They send word: before he died, your father asked you to forgive us. Then they come in person and fall down at his feet. And Joseph…
screen: `IT'S FINE. (IT ISN'T.)` → `THE FATHER IS DEAD.` → `THE BROTHERS PANIC.`

segments.voice: Joseph weeps. Genesis gives him tears before it gives him a word. Here's what makes that strange: he had already forgiven them. Years before, when he first told them who he was, he wept so loudly the Egyptians heard, and he told them not to be grieved or angry with themselves. The decision was made back then. Now the fear is back, and so are his tears. So he makes the decision again, out loud. Fear not, he tells them. You thought evil against me, but God turned it into good. And he comforts them and speaks kindly to them. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't say it never happened; he names it as evil. Forgiving doesn't rewrite the past. It decides what happens next. Jesus does the same on the cross, before anyone says sorry at all. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." One to tell a friend tonight: Jesus forgave from the cross with no apology in sight. Luke says the soldiers went right on casting lots for his clothes, and the rulers went on scoffing. Nothing had been fixed or explained. In both scenes the feelings come and go, like weather over a house. The choice is the house. It comes first, and it holds.
screen: `JOSEPH WEEPS FIRST.` · `HE HAD FORGIVEN THEM YEARS BEFORE.` · `YOU THOUGHT EVIL; GOD TURNED IT TO GOOD.` · `FATHER, FORGIVE THEM.` · then, large: `DECIDE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Let one name come to mind, someone you're still sore at, not the deepest wound. Say it quietly, out loud: I decide to forgive, and then the name. The feeling may lag behind, the way Joseph's tears came back years later. If you pray, you can add the words from the cross: Father, forgive them.
Practicing forgiveness. Choosing to release a debt, and choosing it again when the hurt returns, even before the heart agrees. Today's word.
Your line: decide first. Joseph wept all over again, and his choice still held. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: mia said sorry for skipping senior night. i said it's fine but i'm still mad. is that fake?
options: Not fake if you mean it as a choice. Joseph decided first, with tears still coming.
Kind of. You can't forgive until you stop being mad, so take it back for now.
It's fine. Forgiving just means acting like senior night never happened at all.
chat.meaning: Joseph's forgiveness was a decision he kept and remade while the tears still came. Forgiving decides what's next; it doesn't wait for the feeling.

Original game: Greek ἄφες (aphes), imperative of aphiēmi, in Luke 23:34 (a verse missing from some early manuscripts; the lesson does not mention this). Confirm spelling and accent.
Practice: 'I decide to forgive' is a spoken intention, not a new prayer; the only prayer offered is the quoted line from Luke 23:34.
